hints: Start with the two outermost walls: that tank is as wide as possible. If you want to beat it with a narrower tank, which wall must be replaced?
Use two pointers at both ends. The water level is limited by the shorter wall, so always move the pointer at the shorter wall inward.

1. Set i = 0, j = n-1, best = 0.
  2. While i < j, compute (j - i) * min(walls[i], walls[j]) and update best.
  3. Move the pointer at the shorter wall one step inward.
  4. Return best.

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: Try every pair of walls and compute the tank size.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.idea: Two pointers from the ends, always discarding the shorter wall since it cannot do better with any narrower partner.

explain: For [2,7,3,1,6,4]: walls 0 and 5 give 5×2 = 10; wall 0 is shorter, so move i. Walls 1 and 5 give 4×4 = 16; wall 5 is shorter, move j. Walls 1 and 4 give 3×6 = 18, the best. The shorter wall caps the height, and moving inward only reduces width, so pairing that short wall with anything closer can never beat what we just measured; it is safe to drop it. When both walls are equal, moving either one is fine.
recognize: Pick two ends to maximise width × min height → two pointers moving the shorter side.
